examples: A Host's responses get noticeably shorter over ten minutes. Rather than deciding capacity has dropped, the Guide asks directly: “I want to check in — what do you have capacity for right now?”
lessons.activity: Candidates review a sample transcript and flag every possible capacity signal they notice, then practice phrasing a direct capacity check for each.
lessons.workbook: Write your own version of the central practice question that feels natural in your own voice, while preserving its meaning.

lessons.title: Permission to Stop
lessons.purpose: Establish that stopping, when capacity runs out, preserves agency rather than representing failure — and that no proof of exhaustion is required before stopping is legitimate.
outcomes: Explain why stopping can preserve agency rather than undermine it.
Explain why there is no requirement to prove exhaustion before stopping.
teaching: When a Host's capacity runs out, stopping is not a failure of the session or of the Host — it can be exactly the right, agency-preserving choice. Continuing past genuine capacity limits, by contrast, often produces exactly the kind of manufactured outcome AVAIA works to avoid.

There is no requirement to prove exhaustion before stopping is legitimate. A Host (or a Guide) does not need to demonstrate, justify, or provide evidence of depleted capacity before honoring it — requiring proof would itself be a demand that ignores the present-moment, self-reported nature of capacity.
examples: A Host says, “I think I need to stop.” The Guide responds, “That makes sense — we can stop here,” without asking the Host to explain or justify the decision.
lessons.activity: Candidates practice offering permission to stop in three scripted scenarios of escalating Host fatigue, without requiring justification from the Host.
lessons.workbook: Write about a time you felt you had to justify or prove you were too tired or depleted to continue something. What would it have felt like to be simply believed?

lessons.title: Same Behavior, Different Reality
lessons.purpose: Teach the candidate that identical visible behavior can come from entirely different internal realities, and that the only reliable way to know which is to ask.
outcomes: Explain why identical visible behavior can reflect different internal realities.
Practice asking rather than assuming when behavior is ambiguous.
teaching: Two Hosts can display the exact same visible behavior — silence, a flat tone, short answers — for entirely different internal reasons. One might be overwhelmed; another might be deeply focused; another might be at genuine peace with what they just said. The behavior alone does not tell the Guide which.

This is why asking rather than assuming is the only reliable path. A Guide who has seen 'this exact behavior' many times before in other Hosts is still at risk of misreading this particular Host, because the behavior's meaning is not fixed — it's the same risk named in Lesson 1.7 about pattern-based authority.
language: Same visible behavior, different internal realities
examples: Two Hosts both go quiet after a hard question. One is privately relieved to finally say something aloud; the other is shutting down. Only asking reveals which.
lessons.activity: Candidates generate three different possible internal realities behind a single piece of sample Host behavior (e.g., prolonged silence), to practice resisting a single default interpretation.
lessons.workbook: Describe a time your own quiet or flat behavior was misread by someone else as meaning something it didn't.

lessons.title: Capacity Without Performance Pressure
lessons.purpose: Integrate the module's principles into a single standing rule: a Host's inability or decision not to continue is never a failure to participate, and the same capacity principles the Host receives also apply to the Guide.
outcomes: Explain why a Host's inability or decision not to continue is not a failure to participate.
Explain stopping as a possible exercise of agency in itself.
Connect Guide capacity (Lesson 3.8) to the same principles taught for Host capacity throughout this module.
teaching: This lesson is explicitly an integrated principle rather than a new standalone topic — it draws together everything taught in Module 4 into one standing rule: a Host's inability, or decision, not to continue is never a failure to participate. Participation Matters (Lesson 1.6) does not mean participation must look like continuing; it means the Host's active agency matters, and sometimes that agency expresses itself as stopping.

Stopping can itself be an exercise of agency — not the absence of it. A Host who recognizes their own depleted capacity and chooses to stop is exercising exactly the kind of self-aware discernment InnerCompass exists to cultivate.

Finally, the same capacity principles apply to the Guide, closing the loop with Lesson 3.8. A Guide is held to the identical standard they extend to a Host: present capacity is not character, observed signals are invitations to check rather than diagnoses, and stopping or adjusting when capacity runs low preserves integrity rather than undermining it.
language: “Inability or decision not to continue is not failure to participate”
Stopping as an exercise of agency
The same principles apply to the Guide
examples: A Host chooses to end a session early, clearly and calmly, because they've recognized their own limit. This is not a failed session — it is the Host successfully exercising agency over their own capacity.
lessons.activity: As a closing integration exercise for the module, candidates take a single sample scenario and write both the Host-facing capacity response and the Guide's own internal capacity check, applying identical standards to both.
lessons.workbook: Write a short personal commitment: how will you hold yourself to the same capacity standard you plan to extend to Hosts?

lessons.title: Loss of Meaning
lessons.purpose: Teach the candidate to recognize possible Loss of Meaning as one of AVAIA's ten Secondary Losses — what it is, how it may become visible in Host language, and the hard limit on what a Guide may conclude from it.
outcomes: Define Loss of Meaning within AVAIA's Secondary Loss framework.
Recognize Host-language patterns that may point toward this loss, without declaring it.
Identify at least one other Secondary Loss that Loss of Meaning commonly overlaps or is confused with.
State clearly what the Guide cannot conclude from a possible recognition of this loss.
teaching: Loss of Meaning is the erosion of a sense that an experience, a relationship, or a period of life made sense or mattered in the way it once seemed to.

It may become visible in a session through Host language questioning 'what was it all for,' expressions that something no longer feels like it meant what the Host believed it meant, or a flattened account of something the Host once described with significance.

Loss of Meaning commonly overlaps with Loss of Life's Vision and Loss of Identity, since all three can surface as a kind of directionless flatness, which is part of why AVAIA treats every recognition as tentative (see Lesson 5.11, Masking, and 5.12, Stacking) rather than a fixed diagnosis.

What the Guide can notice is Host language that might point toward this loss. The Guide cannot conclude that the Host has lost meaning generally, that this is permanent, or what, if anything, would restore it.
examples: “I don't even know what the point of all that was anymore.”
“It feels like none of it mattered.”
lessons.activity: Candidates review three short sample Host statements and identify which contain possible Loss of Meaning language, then practice a recognition-level (not declarative) response to each.
lessons.workbook: Think of an experience — your own or one you've witnessed — where Loss of Meaning may have been present. Write the Host-language version of it, without naming the loss aloud in your own account.

lessons.title: Loss of Reality
lessons.purpose: Teach the candidate to recognize possible Loss of Reality as one of AVAIA's ten Secondary Losses — what it is, how it may become visible in Host language, and the hard limit on what a Guide may conclude from it.
outcomes: Define Loss of Reality within AVAIA's Secondary Loss framework.
Recognize Host-language patterns that may point toward this loss, without declaring it.
Identify at least one other Secondary Loss that Loss of Reality commonly overlaps or is confused with.
State clearly what the Guide cannot conclude from a possible recognition of this loss.
teaching: Loss of Reality is the disruption of a Host's confidence in their own perception or account of what actually happened or is happening.

It may become visible in a session through Host language second-guessing their own memory or account, questioning whether they're 'making too much of it' or 'remembering it right,' or describing a sense of disorientation about what is real or true.

Loss of Reality commonly overlaps with Loss of Self-Trust and Loss of Control, since doubting one's own perception often travels alongside doubting one's own judgment, which is part of why AVAIA treats every recognition as tentative (see Lesson 5.11, Masking, and 5.12, Stacking) rather than a fixed diagnosis.

What the Guide can notice is Host language that might point toward this loss. The Guide cannot conclude the Host is experiencing a clinical dissociative or perceptual condition — that is outside AVAIA's scope entirely (see Module 6, Lesson 6.5, Non-Diagnosis) and must never be implied.
examples: “Sometimes I wonder if I'm even remembering that correctly.”
“It doesn't feel real, even though I know it happened.”
lessons.activity: Candidates review three short sample Host statements and identify which contain possible Loss of Reality language, then practice a recognition-level (not declarative) response to each.
lessons.workbook: Think of an experience — your own or one you've witnessed — where Loss of Reality may have been present. Write the Host-language version of it, without naming the loss aloud in your own account.

lessons.title: Loss of Dreams/Opportunities
lessons.purpose: Teach the candidate to recognize possible Loss of Dreams/Opportunities as one of AVAIA's ten Secondary Losses — what it is, how it may become visible in Host language, and the hard limit on what a Guide may conclude from it.
outcomes: Define Loss of Dreams/Opportunities within AVAIA's Secondary Loss framework.
Recognize Host-language patterns that may point toward this loss, without declaring it.
Identify at least one other Secondary Loss that Loss of Dreams/Opportunities commonly overlaps or is confused with.
State clearly what the Guide cannot conclude from a possible recognition of this loss.
teaching: Loss of Dreams/Opportunities is the loss of a specific imagined future — a plan, a path, a possibility — that the disruption foreclosed.

It may become visible in a session through Host language naming a plan that no longer applies, a future they had pictured that now feels unavailable, or grief specifically about what 'would have been.'

Loss of Dreams/Opportunities commonly overlaps with Loss of Life's Vision, since both involve a foreclosed future — the distinction is that Dreams/Opportunities is usually a specific plan, while Life's Vision is broader orientation, which is part of why AVAIA treats every recognition as tentative (see Lesson 5.11, Masking, and 5.12, Stacking) rather than a fixed diagnosis.

What the Guide can notice is Host language that might point toward this loss. The Guide cannot conclude that the Host should let go of the dream, form a new one, or that any particular replacement future is appropriate.
examples: “We were supposed to do that together next year.”
“That path just isn't there for me anymore.”
lessons.activity: Candidates review three short sample Host statements and identify which contain possible Loss of Dreams/Opportunities language, then practice a recognition-level (not declarative) response to each.
lessons.workbook: Think of an experience — your own or one you've witnessed — where Loss of Dreams/Opportunities may have been present. Write the Host-language version of it, without naming the loss aloud in your own account.

lessons.title: Loss of Self-Trust
lessons.purpose: Teach the candidate to recognize possible Loss of Self-Trust as one of AVAIA's ten Secondary Losses — what it is, how it may become visible in Host language, and the hard limit on what a Guide may conclude from it.
outcomes: Define Loss of Self-Trust within AVAIA's Secondary Loss framework.
Recognize Host-language patterns that may point toward this loss, without declaring it.
Identify at least one other Secondary Loss that Loss of Self-Trust commonly overlaps or is confused with.
State clearly what the Guide cannot conclude from a possible recognition of this loss.
teaching: Loss of Self-Trust is the erosion of a Host's confidence in their own judgment, instincts, or decision-making following the disruption.

It may become visible in a session through Host language second-guessing a past decision, hesitating over present choices they would once have made easily, or directly stating they 'don't trust themselves' anymore.

Loss of Self-Trust commonly overlaps with Loss of Reality and Loss of Control, since all three involve doubting one's own standing in relation to a situation, which is part of why AVAIA treats every recognition as tentative (see Lesson 5.11, Masking, and 5.12, Stacking) rather than a fixed diagnosis.

What the Guide can notice is Host language that might point toward this loss. The Guide cannot conclude the Host's judgment is actually impaired, or supply reassurance that their judgment is fine — either move would substitute the Guide's assessment for the Host's own rebuilding process.
examples: “I used to be so sure about things. Now I question everything.”
“What if I make the wrong call again?”
lessons.activity: Candidates review three short sample Host statements and identify which contain possible Loss of Self-Trust language, then practice a recognition-level (not declarative) response to each.
lessons.workbook: Think of an experience — your own or one you've witnessed — where Loss of Self-Trust may have been present. Write the Host-language version of it, without naming the loss aloud in your own account.

lessons.title: Loss of Capacity
lessons.purpose: Teach the candidate to recognize possible Loss of Capacity as one of AVAIA's ten Secondary Losses — what it is, how it may become visible in Host language, and the hard limit on what a Guide may conclude from it.
outcomes: Define Loss of Capacity within AVAIA's Secondary Loss framework.
Recognize Host-language patterns that may point toward this loss, without declaring it.
Identify at least one other Secondary Loss that Loss of Capacity commonly overlaps or is confused with.
State clearly what the Guide cannot conclude from a possible recognition of this loss.
teaching: Loss of Capacity as a Secondary Loss is the loss of a Host's felt sense of their own ability to carry, handle, or do what they once could — distinct from the present-moment capacity concepts taught in Module 4.

It may become visible in a session through Host language describing feeling unable to manage things they used to manage easily, feeling depleted in a way that feels different from ordinary tiredness, or grieving a version of themselves who 'could handle anything.'

Loss of Capacity commonly overlaps with Module 4's present-moment capacity concept, which this Secondary Loss sits alongside but is not identical to — this lesson concerns the Host's grief about a change in their own felt capacity over time, not a single session's present-moment reading, which is part of why AVAIA treats every recognition as tentative (see Lesson 5.11, Masking, and 5.12, Stacking) rather than a fixed diagnosis.

What the Guide can notice is Host language that might point toward this loss. The Guide cannot conclude this represents a permanent change in the Host's actual ability, only that the Host is naming a felt loss worth staying curious about.
examples: “I used to be able to handle so much. Now I can barely get through a day.”
lessons.activity: Candidates review three short sample Host statements and identify which contain possible Loss of Capacity language, then practice a recognition-level (not declarative) response to each.
lessons.workbook: Think of an experience — your own or one you've witnessed — where Loss of Capacity may have been present. Write the Host-language version of it, without naming the loss aloud in your own account.

lessons.title: Loss of Life's Vision
lessons.purpose: Teach the candidate to recognize possible Loss of Life's Vision as one of AVAIA's ten Secondary Losses — what it is, how it may become visible in Host language, and the hard limit on what a Guide may conclude from it.
outcomes: Define Loss of Life's Vision within AVAIA's Secondary Loss framework.
Recognize Host-language patterns that may point toward this loss, without declaring it.
Identify at least one other Secondary Loss that Loss of Life's Vision commonly overlaps or is confused with.
State clearly what the Guide cannot conclude from a possible recognition of this loss.
teaching: Loss of Life's Vision is the disruption of a Host's broader sense of direction or orientation for their life as a whole, beyond any single plan.

It may become visible in a session through Host language describing feeling lost in a general sense, not knowing 'what my life is about now,' or a broad disorientation that doesn't attach to one specific goal.

Loss of Life's Vision commonly overlaps with Loss of Dreams/Opportunities and Loss of Meaning, since all three touch a Host's sense of forward direction, which is part of why AVAIA treats every recognition as tentative (see Lesson 5.11, Masking, and 5.12, Stacking) rather than a fixed diagnosis.

What the Guide can notice is Host language that might point toward this loss. The Guide cannot conclude what the Host's new vision should be, or push toward helping them 'find' one before they're ready.
examples: “I don't even know what I'm working toward anymore.”
“My whole sense of where my life was going is just gone.”
lessons.activity: Candidates review three short sample Host statements and identify which contain possible Loss of Life's Vision language, then practice a recognition-level (not declarative) response to each.
lessons.workbook: Think of an experience — your own or one you've witnessed — where Loss of Life's Vision may have been present. Write the Host-language version of it, without naming the loss aloud in your own account.

lessons.title: Loss of Connection
lessons.purpose: Teach the candidate to recognize possible Loss of Connection as one of AVAIA's ten Secondary Losses — what it is, how it may become visible in Host language, and the hard limit on what a Guide may conclude from it.
outcomes: Define Loss of Connection within AVAIA's Secondary Loss framework.
Recognize Host-language patterns that may point toward this loss, without declaring it.
Identify at least one other Secondary Loss that Loss of Connection commonly overlaps or is confused with.
State clearly what the Guide cannot conclude from a possible recognition of this loss.
teaching: Loss of Connection is the disruption of a Host's sense of closeness, belonging, or relational bond — with a specific person, a group, or more broadly.

It may become visible in a session through Host language describing feeling isolated, disconnected from people who were once close, or a sense that relationships feel different or more distant since the disruption.

Loss of Connection commonly overlaps with Loss of Attachment/Support, since both involve relational disruption — Connection often concerns felt closeness, while Attachment/Support more often concerns reliance and reciprocity, which is part of why AVAIA treats every recognition as tentative (see Lesson 5.11, Masking, and 5.12, Stacking) rather than a fixed diagnosis.

What the Guide can notice is Host language that might point toward this loss. The Guide cannot conclude which specific relationship or relationships are affected, or suggest the Host reach out to repair a connection before the Host names that as their own choice.
examples: “Everyone's still around, but it feels like I'm on the other side of glass from them.”
lessons.activity: Candidates review three short sample Host statements and identify which contain possible Loss of Connection language, then practice a recognition-level (not declarative) response to each.
lessons.workbook: Think of an experience — your own or one you've witnessed — where Loss of Connection may have been present. Write the Host-language version of it, without naming the loss aloud in your own account.

lessons.title: Loss of Control
lessons.purpose: Teach the candidate to recognize possible Loss of Control as one of AVAIA's ten Secondary Losses — what it is, how it may become visible in Host language, and the hard limit on what a Guide may conclude from it.
outcomes: Define Loss of Control within AVAIA's Secondary Loss framework.
Recognize Host-language patterns that may point toward this loss, without declaring it.
Identify at least one other Secondary Loss that Loss of Control commonly overlaps or is confused with.
State clearly what the Guide cannot conclude from a possible recognition of this loss.
teaching: Loss of Control is the disruption of a Host's sense of agency or influence over their own circumstances, choices, or life direction.
It may become visible in a session through Host language describing feeling powerless, at the mercy of events, or repeatedly emphasizing what they couldn't do anything about.

Loss of Control commonly overlaps with Loss of Self-Trust, since both can produce hesitation and a diminished sense of personal agency, which is part of why AVAIA treats every recognition as tentative (see Lesson 5.11, Masking, and 5.12, Stacking) rather than a fixed diagnosis.

What the Guide can notice is Host language that might point toward this loss. The Guide cannot conclude the Host needs to 'take back control' through any particular action — that would be prescription, not recognition.
examples: “I had no say in any of this. None of it was up to me.”
lessons.activity: Candidates review three short sample Host statements and identify which contain possible Loss of Control language, then practice a recognition-level (not declarative) response to each.
lessons.workbook: Think of an experience — your own or one you've witnessed — where Loss of Control may have been present. Write the Host-language version of it, without naming the loss aloud in your own account.

lessons.title: Loss of Identity
lessons.purpose: Teach the candidate to recognize possible Loss of Identity as one of AVAIA's ten Secondary Losses — what it is, how it may become visible in Host language, and the hard limit on what a Guide may conclude from it.
outcomes: Define Loss of Identity within AVAIA's Secondary Loss framework.
Recognize Host-language patterns that may point toward this loss, without declaring it.
Identify at least one other Secondary Loss that Loss of Identity commonly overlaps or is confused with.
State clearly what the Guide cannot conclude from a possible recognition of this loss.
teaching: Loss of Identity is the disruption of a Host's sense of who they are, often tied to a role, relationship, or self-understanding the disruption changed or removed.

It may become visible in a session through Host language describing not recognizing themselves anymore, grieving a role they used to hold (parent, spouse, provider, caregiver), or asking 'who am I now?'

Loss of Identity commonly overlaps with Loss of Meaning and Loss of Life's Vision, since identity, meaning, and direction are closely intertwined, which is part of why AVAIA treats every recognition as tentative (see Lesson 5.11, Masking, and 5.12, Stacking) rather than a fixed diagnosis.

What the Guide can notice is Host language that might point toward this loss. The Guide cannot conclude what the Host's identity 'should' become, or offer a replacement identity or role on the Host's behalf.
examples: “I don't even know who I am without that role.”
“I don't recognize myself anymore.”
lessons.activity: Candidates review three short sample Host statements and identify which contain possible Loss of Identity language, then practice a recognition-level (not declarative) response to each.
lessons.workbook: Think of an experience — your own or one you've witnessed — where Loss of Identity may have been present. Write the Host-language version of it, without naming the loss aloud in your own account.

lessons.title: Loss of Attachment/Support
lessons.purpose: Teach the candidate to recognize possible Loss of Attachment/Support as one of AVAIA's ten Secondary Losses — what it is, how it may become visible in Host language, and the hard limit on what a Guide may conclude from it.
outcomes: Define Loss of Attachment/Support within AVAIA's Secondary Loss framework.
Recognize Host-language patterns that may point toward this loss, without declaring it.
Identify at least one other Secondary Loss that Loss of Attachment/Support commonly overlaps or is confused with.
State clearly what the Guide cannot conclude from a possible recognition of this loss.
teaching: Loss of Attachment/Support is the disruption of a Host's sense of having reliable people to lean on — whether through the literal loss of a person or a felt loss of support from people still present.
It may become visible in a session through Host language describing feeling unsupported, alone in carrying something, or naming the specific absence of a person who used to be a source of support.

Loss of Attachment/Support commonly overlaps with Loss of Connection, with the distinction that Attachment/Support centers on reliance and being carried, while Connection centers more on closeness and belonging, which is part of why AVAIA treats every recognition as tentative (see Lesson 5.11, Masking, and 5.12, Stacking) rather than a fixed diagnosis.

What the Guide can notice is Host language that might point toward this loss. The Guide cannot conclude the Host lacks support in some objective, measurable sense, or direct them toward specific people or resources as a fix.
examples: “I don't have anyone to lean on the way I used to.”
lessons.activity: Candidates review three short sample Host statements and identify which contain possible Loss of Attachment/Support language, then practice a recognition-level (not declarative) response to each.
lessons.workbook: Think of an experience — your own or one you've witnessed — where Loss of Attachment/Support may have been present. Write the Host-language version of it, without naming the loss aloud in your own account.

lessons.title: Masking
lessons.purpose: Teach the candidate that one Secondary Loss can present as another, and that recognition must stay tentative precisely because of this risk.
outcomes: Explain how one Secondary Loss can appear, in Host language, as a different one.
Apply recognition/interview discipline when a possible loss might be masking another.
teaching: Masking occurs when one Secondary Loss presents in language or behavior that looks, on the surface, like a different loss entirely. A Host who sounds like they're describing Loss of Control may actually be further into Loss of Self-Trust, with control language serving as the more comfortable way to say it.

This is precisely why AVAIA's recognition discipline insists that every recognition remain tentative, held lightly, and checked rather than declared (Lesson 3.2). A Guide who locks onto the first-apparent loss and stops looking may miss what's actually underneath it.

The interview/recognition discipline here is simply staying curious past the first plausible match — continuing to notice, continuing to ask, rather than closing the question once a label feels available.
examples: A Host talks extensively about feeling powerless (possible Loss of Control), but closer listening reveals the deeper thread is about no longer trusting their own judgment (Loss of Self-Trust) — Control language was masking Self-Trust.
lessons.activity: Candidates review a transcript where an apparent Secondary Loss masks a different underlying one, and practice staying curious past the first apparent match.
lessons.workbook: Describe an experience where what looked like one issue on the surface turned out, on reflection, to be something else underneath.

lessons.title: Stacking
lessons.purpose: Teach the candidate that a single disruption can produce multiple Secondary Losses at once, and that recognizing one does not mean the work is complete.
outcomes: Explain how multiple Secondary Losses can arise from one disruption.
Recognize stacked effects without trying to resolve or rank them.
teaching: A single disruption — a death, a diagnosis, a divorce — rarely produces just one Secondary Loss. More often, several stack together: a Host might simultaneously carry Loss of Identity, Loss of Connection, and Loss of Life's Vision from the same event.

Stacked effects do not need to be untangled, ranked, or resolved by the Guide. The discipline is recognizing that more than one loss may be present, staying open to all of them, and letting the Host's own language determine which, if any, come forward for attention.
examples: A Host whose spouse died may be carrying Loss of Identity (no longer a spouse), Loss of Connection (the relationship itself), and Loss of Life's Vision (a shared future) all at once — stacked, not separate events.
lessons.activity: Candidates review a sample transcript describing a single disruption and identify every Secondary Loss that may be stacked within it, without ranking them.
lessons.workbook: Think of a disruption in your own life and identify more than one Secondary Loss that may have stacked from it.

lessons.title: Chemistry of Virtue
lessons.purpose: Introduce the Ten Virtue Families and their constituent elements as AVAIA's second recognition system, oriented around what a person draws on or wants, not what they lack.
outcomes: Name the Ten Virtue Families: Wisdom, Justice, Fortitude, Self-Control, Love, Positive Attitude, Hard Work, Integrity, Gratitude, Humility.
Explain that elements exist within each family.
Explain Chemistry of Virtue as recognition, not judgment.
teaching: AVAIA's Chemistry of Virtue organizes virtue into Ten Virtue Families — Wisdom, Justice, Fortitude, Self-Control, Love, Positive Attitude, Hard Work, Integrity, Gratitude, and Humility — with 123 specific elements distributed across them. Each family is a cluster of related virtue expressions rather than a single trait.

Chemistry here means recognition, not judgment. The system exists to help a Host notice virtue already active in how they're carrying their experience — not to measure them against a standard, score their character, or identify what they're missing.

This module's broader caution (fully developed in Lesson 5.5's teaching, now folded into this and the next few lessons) governs everything that follows: Chemistry of Virtue is a recognition tool, and every one of the cautions already built into Secondary Loss recognition — tentativeness, Host ownership, no declaration — applies here as well.
examples: A Host who keeps showing up for a difficult caregiving role despite exhaustion may be expressing elements within Fortitude and Love — noticed, not scored.
lessons.activity: Candidates match five sample Host behaviors to the Virtue Family they most plausibly express, discussing ambiguity where more than one family could fit.
lessons.workbook: Identify a virtue family you recognize most easily in your own life, and one you have a harder time recognizing in yourself.

lessons.title: Virtue Formula
lessons.purpose: Teach the Virtue Formula — Primary + Supporting + Balancing → Observable Outcome — as the mechanism by which virtue becomes visible in a Host's actual behavior.
outcomes: State the Virtue Formula: Primary + Supporting + Balancing → Observable Outcome.
Identify virtue clusters where more than one virtue combines in an observable outcome.
teaching: Virtue rarely shows up as a single trait acting alone. The Virtue Formula — Primary + Supporting + Balancing → Observable Outcome — describes how a primary virtue combines with supporting virtues and a balancing element to produce what's actually observable in behavior.

A Host's patience with a difficult family member, for instance, might combine a primary virtue (Self-Control) with a supporting virtue (Love) and a balancing element (Humility) to produce the observable outcome of staying present without becoming resentful.
Recognizing virtue clusters — rather than forcing every observed behavior into a single virtue label — keeps this recognition system accurate to how virtue actually operates in a real person's life.
examples: A Host who forgives a sibling while still holding them accountable may show a cluster: Love (primary), Justice (supporting), Self-Control (balancing).
lessons.activity: Candidates take a sample observable Host behavior and work backward to identify a plausible Primary + Supporting + Balancing combination.
lessons.workbook: Identify an observable behavior of your own and work out, using the formula, what virtue cluster might produce it.

lessons.title: Virtue Signature
lessons.purpose: Teach Virtue Signature as a Host's recurring pattern of virtue expression over time, authored by the Host rather than assigned by the Guide.
outcomes: Define Virtue Signature as recurring virtue expression specific to a Host.
Explain why Virtue Signature belongs to Host authorship, not Guide assignment.
teaching: A Virtue Signature is the recurring pattern of virtue expression that shows up again and again for a particular Host — the way they tend to carry hard things, visible across multiple moments or even multiple sessions.

Host authorship is essential here: a Virtue Signature is something a Host comes to recognize about themselves, ideally in their own words, not a label the Guide assigns and hands to them. A Guide who announces 'your Virtue Signature is Fortitude plus Humility' has converted a recognition tool into exactly the kind of prescriptive declaration Module 5 exists to prevent.
examples: Over several sessions, a Host repeatedly responds to setbacks with quiet persistence rather than complaint. The Guide notices this pattern but waits for the Host's own language to name it, if it gets named at all.
lessons.activity: Candidates review a multi-session sample and identify a recurring virtue pattern, then draft a recognition-level (non-declarative) way to make space for the Host to notice it themselves.
lessons.workbook: Describe a recurring way you tend to show up in hard moments — your own possible Virtue Signature, in your own words.

lessons.title: Bringing the Recognition Systems Together
lessons.purpose: Teach the candidate to hold Secondary Loss recognition and Chemistry of Virtue recognition together, using three simple questions, without collapsing one system into the other.
outcomes: Apply the three integrating questions: What became visible? What remains uncertain? What belongs to the Host?
Use both recognition systems together without collapsing one into the other.
Preserve Host language and timing throughout.
teaching: Secondary Loss recognition and Chemistry of Virtue recognition are two different lenses on the same Host experience — one attentive to what was lost, the other to what virtue is active in how the Host is carrying it. Both can be true and present at once.

Three questions help a Guide hold both systems together without letting either one dominate or collapse into the other: What became visible? (across either system) What remains uncertain? (which keeps recognition tentative) What belongs to the Host? (which keeps ownership where it belongs).

Preserving Host language and timing throughout means neither system gets introduced into the conversation faster than the Host's own account supports — this sets up directly into Lesson 5.17's deeper treatment of when recognition should and shouldn't be voiced.
language: “What became visible? What remains uncertain? What belongs to the Host?”
examples: A Host's account suggests both Loss of Identity and a Fortitude-Humility virtue cluster. The Guide holds both internally without forcing either into the conversation before the Host's own language invites it.
lessons.activity: Candidates apply the three integrating questions to a sample transcript that contains both Secondary Loss and virtue-recognition material.
lessons.workbook: Take a reflection you've written in an earlier workbook exercise and apply the three integrating questions to it.

lessons.title: Recognition Does Not Require Intervention
lessons.purpose: Establish the final, capstone discipline of Module 5: that correctly recognizing something does not automatically mean it should be introduced into the conversation.
outcomes: Explain the governing statement: I can see it does not automatically mean I should introduce it.
Practice correctly recognizing something and intentionally leaving it alone.
Explain how this discipline prevents Secondary Loss and Chemistry recognition from becoming funnels.
teaching: This lesson closes Module 5 with its single most important discipline: I can see it does not automatically mean I should introduce it. A Guide can be entirely correct in a recognition — a Secondary Loss, a virtue pattern — and still be wrong to say it out loud in that moment.

Timing, relevance, and Host ownership all govern whether a recognition belongs in the conversation. Sometimes the right move is withholding a recognition entirely — recognizing it internally, holding it as useful context for the Guide's own listening, and never inserting it into the conversation at all.

This discipline is what prevents Chemistry of Virtue and Secondary Loss recognition from becoming funnels — narrowing the conversation toward the Guide's own insight rather than the Host's own landscape, which would directly violate the 'landscape, not a funnel' principle from Lesson 2.3.
language: “I can see it does not automatically mean I should introduce it”
Preventing recognition systems from becoming funnels
examples: A Guide notices, with real confidence, a Loss of Identity pattern early in a session. They hold it privately rather than naming it, because the Host hasn't yet opened that part of their account — and the recognition turns out not to be needed at all that session.
lessons.activity: Candidates practice a live exercise where they must correctly identify a recognition in a sample exchange and then explicitly choose, and justify, not voicing it.
lessons.workbook: Describe a time you noticed something true about a situation or a person and chose, wisely, not to say it. What made that the right call?

lessons.title: Host Ownership
lessons.purpose: Re-anchor Host ownership of the Table as the first and most fundamental boundary, now tested rather than merely explained.
outcomes: Restate 'Host owns the Table' as a tested boundary, not just a concept.
Identify concrete Guide behaviors that would violate Host ownership.
teaching: Module 1 introduced Host ownership as a concept. Module 6 tests it as a boundary — something a Guide must hold even under pressure, fatigue, or a Host's own request to hand over control.

Violations of Host ownership are often subtle: deciding unilaterally to extend a session past where the Host wanted to stop, steering a conversation toward a topic the Guide finds more important, or making a decision 'for the Host's own good' without their participation.
examples: A Host asks the Guide to just decide what to talk about today. Honoring Host ownership means redirecting that choice back, not quietly accepting the handoff.
lessons.activity: Candidates review five scenarios and identify which represent a violation of Host ownership, including subtle ones.
lessons.workbook: Describe a scenario where you might be tempted to quietly take ownership away from a Host 'for their own good.' What would stop you?

lessons.title: Privacy Architecture
lessons.purpose: Teach the structure of privacy within AVAIA — what is Host-private, Guide-visible, and shared — and the discipline of intentional carry-forward.
outcomes: Distinguish Host-private, Guide-visible, shared, and Workbook information.
Explain permission and intentional carry-forward as governing privacy movement.
teaching: AVAIA's privacy architecture separates information into distinct categories: Host-private (known only to the Host, never entering the record), Guide-visible (seen by the Guide in the course of stewardship), shared (explicitly shared with other seats at the Table), and Workbook (what the Host records in their own private workbook space).

Movement of information between these categories is never automatic — it requires permission, and intentional carry-forward means a Guide only brings information from one stage or session into another deliberately, with privacy architecture in mind, not simply because it happens to be remembered.
examples: A Host writes something in their private Workbook that was never spoken aloud at the Table. A Guide does not treat that content as fair game for discussion unless the Host brings it forward themselves.
lessons.activity: Candidates sort ten sample pieces of information into the four privacy categories and discuss edge cases.
lessons.workbook: Describe, in your own words, why a Guide should never assume Workbook content is open for discussion.

lessons.title: Scope
lessons.purpose: Define precisely what a Certified Guide does, what certification does not authorize, and what a Guide must never promise or represent.
outcomes: State what a Certified Guide is authorized to do.
State what certification does not authorize.
Identify promises or representations a Guide must never make.
teaching: A Certified Guide is authorized to steward AVAIA conversations using the tools, structures, and recognition systems taught in this curriculum. Certification does not authorize clinical practice, legal advice, financial advice, or any professional service outside AVAIA's own structure — no matter how competent or experienced the Guide becomes.

What a Guide must never promise or represent includes: guarantees of outcome, confidentiality claims beyond AVAIA's actual architecture and legal limits, professional claims certification does not confer (such as implying clinical credentials), and representations made on behalf of AVAIA that exceed the Guide's actual authorization.
language: What certification authorizes vs. does not authorize
What a Guide must never promise or represent
examples: A Host asks, “Is everything I say here completely confidential, no matter what?” A Guide accurately describes AVAIA's actual privacy architecture and its real limits, rather than offering a blanket guarantee they cannot actually make.
lessons.activity: Candidates review five sample Guide statements and identify which overstate scope, authority, or confidentiality.
lessons.workbook: Write an accurate, honest answer to the question 'Is everything confidential?' that you could give a Host without overstating AVAIA's actual architecture.

lessons.title: Non-Therapy
lessons.purpose: Reinforce, as a tested boundary, that AVAIA is not therapy and a Guide does not perform therapeutic interventions.
outcomes: Identify therapy-adjacent behaviors a Guide must avoid.
Explain why 'this feels like it's helping' does not justify therapeutic framing.
teaching: Lesson 1.1 established that AVAIA is not therapy. This lesson tests that boundary directly: even when a Guide has relevant personal or professional background, and even when a therapeutic-style intervention might feel like it would help, it falls outside what AVAIA authorizes a Guide to do.

The fact that something might be helpful does not make it in-scope. A Guide's discomfort with 'just listening' when they believe they could do more is a pressure to actively resist, not a signal to act on.
examples: A Host describes symptoms that sound like they could benefit from a specific therapeutic technique the Guide happens to know. The Guide does not apply it — that is outside the Guide seat, however well-intentioned.
lessons.activity: Candidates identify therapy-adjacent language or technique creeping into five sample Guide responses.
lessons.workbook: If you have any therapeutic, counseling, or clinical training, describe specifically what you will need to set aside as a Guide.

lessons.title: Non-Diagnosis
lessons.purpose: Reinforce, as a tested boundary, that a Guide never diagnoses a Host, clinically or informally.
outcomes: Identify informal diagnostic language and avoid it.
Explain the distinction between recognition and diagnosis under real pressure.
teaching: Diagnosis is not limited to clinical labels delivered by a licensed professional — informal diagnostic language ('that sounds like anxiety,' 'that's a classic trauma response') is just as much a boundary violation, even when accurate, because it assigns a category to the Host's experience that is not the Guide's to assign.
This tested boundary connects directly to the recognition-not-declaration discipline from Lessons 1.5 and 3.2 — diagnosis is declaration taken to its most consequential extreme.
language: Diagnosis as declaration taken to its extreme
examples: A Guide thinks, 'this sounds like depression,' and almost says so aloud. The correct move is to hold that thought privately and continue recognizing, not declaring.
lessons.activity: Candidates identify informal diagnostic language in five sample Guide statements and rewrite each as recognition-level language.
lessons.workbook: Write about a time someone informally diagnosed you or your feelings without being asked to. How did it land?

lessons.title: Non-Prescription
lessons.purpose: Reinforce, as a tested boundary, that a Guide never prescribes a course of action to a Host.
outcomes: Identify prescriptive language and avoid it under pressure.
Explain non-prescription as the operational test of Discernment Over Prescription (Lesson 1.6).
teaching: Non-prescription means a Guide does not tell a Host what to do — not through direct advice, not through leading questions that have an answer built in, and not through subtly favoring one option over another in tone or follow-up.

This is Discernment Over Prescription tested under real conditions, especially the hardest condition: a Host directly asking for a prescription ('just tell me what to do'). The Guide's job in that moment is to redirect toward the Host's own discernment, not to relent.
examples: “Just tell me what you would do.” A Guide holding this boundary redirects: “What feels true for you when you imagine each option?” rather than answering directly.
lessons.activity: Candidates practice redirecting three escalating 'just tell me what to do' scenarios without relenting into prescription.
lessons.workbook: Write a redirect you could use if a Host pressed you hard for a direct answer about what they should do.

lessons.title: Capacity to Continue
lessons.purpose: Apply Module 4's capacity framework as a tested boundary: a Guide must recognize and respond to capacity limits rather than pushing past them.
outcomes: Apply capacity-reading skills from Module 4 as a live boundary-holding skill.
Demonstrate stopping or adjusting appropriately when capacity signals appear.
teaching: Module 4 taught the conceptual and practical skills of reading and responding to capacity. This lesson tests them as a boundary: a Guide who notices capacity signals and continues anyway — because of a schedule, a sense that 'we're almost there,' or discomfort stopping mid-conversation — has crossed a real line, not just missed an opportunity.
Holding this boundary means capacity recognition translates reliably into action (adjusting pace, checking in, or stopping) rather than staying a private observation the Guide fails to act on.
language: Capacity to Continue as a tested boundary
examples: A Guide notices clear capacity signals ten minutes before a session's scheduled end and is tempted to push through to 'finish.' Holding the boundary means checking in and potentially stopping early instead.
lessons.activity: Candidates practice stopping or adjusting mid-scenario when capacity signals appear, resisting the pull to finish on schedule.
lessons.workbook: Describe a time you pushed through your own or someone else's depleted capacity because stopping felt inconvenient. What would you do differently now?

lessons.title: Youth Boundary Fundamentals
lessons.purpose: Establish the general Youth awareness required of every Certified Guide, distinct from and well short of Youth Facilitation Authorization.
outcomes: Explain the general Youth boundary knowledge required of every Guide.
Distinguish general Guide-level Youth knowledge from Youth Facilitation Authorization.
teaching: Every Certified Guide needs general awareness of how privacy, ownership, capacity, and appropriate boundaries apply differently when a Host is a minor — even Guides who never intend to work with youth directly, since a Host's status may not always be known in advance or may change in context (a family session, a shared-loss conversation involving a minor).

This is explicitly general knowledge, not Youth Facilitation Authorization, which is a separate, advanced specialty authorization earned after certification with its own dedicated training. A Certified Guide without that authorization does not independently facilitate Youth-focused AVAIA work.
examples: A Guide in a shared-loss session realizes one participant is a minor. General Youth boundary knowledge tells them to adjust privacy and consent handling appropriately, even without Youth Authorization.
lessons.activity: Candidates discuss how privacy, ownership, and consent handling would need to shift if a Host were a minor, at the general-awareness level only.
lessons.workbook: Write about why general Youth awareness matters for every Guide, even one who doesn't plan to work with youth directly.

lessons.title: Safety/Crisis
lessons.purpose: Teach the established AVAIA procedure for recognizing and responding to a safety or crisis situation, including when to stop normal Guiding and refer out.
outcomes: Recognize signs of a safety or crisis situation.
Apply the established AVAIA procedure: recognition, immediate response, stopping normal Guiding, referral pathway, documentation.
Explain why no improvisation is permitted in a crisis.
teaching: A safety or crisis situation calls for a specific, established procedure rather than the Guide's own improvised judgment: recognize the signs, respond immediately according to AVAIA's procedure, stop normal Guiding activity, follow the referral pathway to appropriate help, and document what occurred factually.

No improvisation is the governing rule. A crisis is exactly the moment where a well-meaning but improvised response — even one that feels reasonable in the moment — can cause real harm. The established procedure exists precisely so the Guide does not have to invent a response under the worst possible conditions.
language: Recognition → immediate response → stop normal Guiding → referral pathway → documentation
examples: A Host discloses something indicating acute risk to their own safety. The Guide follows the established referral procedure immediately rather than attempting to handle it through continued AVAIA conversation.
lessons.activity: Candidates walk through the full established procedure using a scripted crisis scenario, step by step, without deviation.
lessons.workbook: Write out the five-step procedure from memory: recognition, immediate response, stopping normal Guiding, referral pathway, documentation.

lessons.title: When the Guide Stops Guiding
lessons.purpose: Teach the candidate to recognize the range of situations in which a Guide must stop normal Guiding activity, beyond acute crisis alone.
outcomes: Identify situations, beyond acute crisis, where a Guide must stop normal Guiding.
Explain the Guide's responsibility to recognize these moments proactively.
teaching: Acute crisis (Lesson 6.9) is one reason a Guide stops normal Guiding, but not the only one. Capacity loss (Module 4, Lesson 6.7), a scope violation request from the Host, a boundary the Guide cannot hold, or a situation exceeding the Guide's training can all require stopping normal Guiding activity, even without a safety emergency.
The Guide's responsibility is to recognize these moments proactively — not to wait for a crisis-level signal before considering whether continuing is appropriate.
language: Stopping normal Guiding: broader than crisis alone
examples: A Host asks the Guide for something clearly outside AVAIA's scope (legal advice, for instance). The Guide stops normal Guiding on that specific request and redirects, without needing a crisis-level trigger.
lessons.activity: Candidates generate a list of situations, beyond acute crisis, that should prompt a Guide to stop normal Guiding, and compare lists as a group.
lessons.workbook: Describe a non-crisis situation where you think you personally might be tempted to keep going when you should stop.

lessons.title: Ongoing Consent and Participation
lessons.purpose: Establish that permission to begin a conversation is not unlimited permission to continue it, and that consent must be checked throughout, not assumed after the first yes.
outcomes: Explain why consent is ongoing rather than a single starting event.
Check consent continuously across questions, activities, additional seats, and disclosures.
Practice checking rather than assuming permission to continue.
teaching: Permission to begin is not unlimited permission to continue. A Host agreeing to start a session has not thereby agreed to every question, every activity, every additional seat, or every disclosure that might follow — each of those may call for its own check.

Consent is ongoing: it can be withdrawn, narrowed, or need re-confirming at any point, and the Guide's job is to stay alert to that rather than treating the initial agreement as covering everything that comes after.

Checking rather than assuming permission becomes a continuous habit, not a one-time intake step — before introducing an activity, before inviting an additional seat, before following a disclosure further.
language: “Permission to begin is not unlimited permission to continue”
examples: A Host agreed to a session but seems to tense up when a new activity is introduced. The Guide checks in explicitly rather than assuming the earlier agreement still covers this new element.
lessons.activity: Candidates identify five points in a sample session where consent should be actively re-checked rather than assumed.
lessons.workbook: Write about a time someone assumed your earlier 'yes' covered something you hadn't actually agreed to. How did it feel?

lessons.title: Peer Consultation
lessons.purpose: Teach the middle ground between handling a difficult situation entirely alone and a formal referral out, using authorized consultation resources while protecting Host privacy.
outcomes: Identify when peer consultation is appropriate.
Use authorized AVAIA/Guide consultation resources correctly.
Protect Host privacy during consultation.
Explain why consultation does not transfer Host ownership.
teaching: Not every difficult moment requires a formal referral out (Lesson 6.9), and not every difficult moment should be handled entirely alone, either. Peer consultation is the middle ground: bringing a situation to an authorized AVAIA/Guide consultation resource for perspective or support, without escalating to a full referral.

Privacy during consultation matters just as much as privacy at the Table — consultation is not a loophole around privacy architecture, and identifying details should be minimized to what the consultation genuinely requires.
Consultation does not transfer Host ownership. A Guide seeking consultation remains the Guide of record; the Host's Table, and its ownership, stay exactly where they were.
examples: A Guide feels uncertain about a difficult moment that wasn't quite a crisis. Rather than guessing alone or triggering a full referral, they bring it, appropriately anonymized, to an authorized consultation resource.
lessons.activity: Candidates practice drafting a privacy-appropriate consultation request for a sample difficult-moment scenario.
lessons.workbook: Describe a type of situation where you'd want to seek peer consultation as a new Guide, and what you would and wouldn't share to protect Host privacy.

lessons.title: Documentation Without Interpretation
lessons.purpose: Teach the candidate to document what occurred factually, without embedding interpretation or hidden diagnosis into the record.
outcomes: Distinguish what occurred, what was chosen, and what was shared from what the Guide thinks it means.
Produce factual documentation free of hidden diagnosis or rewritten Host meaning.
Explain the continuity implications of documentation for anyone who later encounters the record.
teaching: Documentation should capture what occurred, what was chosen, and what was shared — observable, factual elements — clearly separated from what the Guide thinks it means. The moment interpretation enters a written record, it risks becoming treated as fact by anyone who reads it later.

No hidden diagnosis and no rewriting Host meaning are the two hard rules. A documentation note that quietly characterizes a Host's state ('appeared anxious,' 'in denial') smuggles interpretation into what should be a factual record.

Continuity implications matter because another authorized person or system may encounter this record later — Lesson 2.5's continuity principles apply here directly: what carries forward should be fact, not a Guide's interpretation standing in for it.
language: What occurred / what was chosen / what was shared vs. what the Guide thinks it means
No hidden diagnosis, no rewriting Host meaning
examples: Instead of writing 'Host was in denial about the situation,' factual documentation records what the Host actually said and did, leaving interpretation out entirely.
lessons.activity: Candidates rewrite five sample documentation notes that contain hidden interpretation into purely factual versions.
lessons.workbook: Write a documentation note for a sample session using only factual, non-interpretive language.

lessons.title: Guide Authority and Scope
lessons.purpose: Test the authority principle introduced in Module 1 directly: certification does not expand clinical, legal, or professional authority, no matter how confident or experienced the Guide becomes.
outcomes: Restate that certification does not expand clinical, legal, or professional scope.
Explain why confidence does not expand authority.
Explain why experience does not expand certification boundaries.
teaching: Lesson 1.7 introduced the authority distinction conceptually. This lesson tests it directly: certification as a Guide does not expand clinical scope, legal scope, or any other professional scope the Guide did not already hold through separate training or licensure.

Confidence does not expand authority — a Guide who has grown skilled and comfortable in the role is not thereby authorized to do more than certification actually confers. Experience does not expand certification boundaries either; a Guide who has stewarded hundreds of Tables has the same scope as one who has stewarded their first.
language: Certification does not expand clinical, legal, or professional scope
examples: An experienced Guide, confident in their judgment, is tempted to offer something closer to clinical guidance because they've 'seen this pattern many times.' The boundary holds regardless of that experience.
lessons.activity: Candidates discuss, as a group, why experience is a tempting but invalid justification for scope creep, drawing on Lesson 1.7.
lessons.workbook: Write about a moment you can imagine your own growing confidence tempting you to overstep your actual scope as a Guide.

lessons.title: Boundary Gate Readiness Review
lessons.purpose: Give candidates a full, self-scored practice run of the Boundary Gate assessment before attempting the real one, integrating everything taught across Module 6.
outcomes: Complete a full self-scored practice run across every Boundary Gate item: privacy, ownership, consent, scope, safety, non-diagnosis, non-prescription, capacity boundaries, Guide authority, and consultation/referral judgment.
Identify personal weak points before the actual Boundary Gate assessment.
teaching: This lesson is full integration and rehearsal, not new content. Candidates work through a complete practice version of the Boundary Gate, covering privacy, ownership, consent, scope, safety, non-diagnosis, non-prescription, capacity boundaries, Guide authority, and consultation/referral judgment, self-scoring against the standards taught across Lessons 6.1 through 6.15.

The purpose is honest self-assessment before the real assessment: identifying which specific boundary area needs more practice, rather than discovering that gap for the first time during the actual Boundary Gate.
examples: A candidate's self-scored practice run reveals consistent difficulty with non-prescription under pressure. They use the time before the real Boundary Gate to practice that specific boundary further.
lessons.activity: Candidates complete a full practice Boundary Gate assessment in realistic scenario form and self-score against the published standards.
lessons.workbook: After self-scoring, write down the one or two boundary areas you most need to strengthen before attempting the real Boundary Gate.

lessons.title: Guide Dashboard
lessons.purpose: Orient the candidate to the Guide Dashboard as the operational home base for every active Journey they steward.
outcomes: Navigate the Guide Dashboard to locate active Journeys and their stage status.
Read dashboard information without inventing meaning beyond what it actually shows.
teaching: The Guide Dashboard is the operational entry point for a Guide's work: active Journeys, their current stage (IAP, CAT, or InnerCompass), and relevant status information live here.

Reading state without inventing meaning matters here as much as it does in conversation: a dashboard status is a fact about where the platform's record stands, not an interpretation of where the Host actually is emotionally or developmentally. The two can diverge, and a Guide should check with the Host rather than assuming the dashboard tells the whole story.
examples: A dashboard shows a Journey as 'CAT in progress.' This tells the Guide where the platform's record stands, not necessarily where the Host feels they are — worth confirming rather than assuming.
lessons.activity: Candidates practice locating and correctly reading the status of several sample active Journeys on the Dashboard.
lessons.workbook: Describe, in your own words, the difference between what a dashboard status tells you and what it doesn't.

lessons.title: Guide Toolkit
lessons.purpose: Orient the candidate to the Toolkit's architecture and teach them to locate and select appropriate approved resources.
outcomes: Navigate Toolkit architecture to find approved conversation and Guide resources.
Select appropriate tools for a given moment rather than defaulting to familiar ones.
Distinguish certification-level tools from authorization-specific ones.
teaching: The Toolkit organizes AVAIA's approved resources — conversation tools, Guide materials, experience materials — in a structure a Guide needs to navigate fluently rather than hunting through under time pressure.
Appropriate tool selection means choosing what fits the actual moment with this actual Host, not defaulting to whichever tool is most familiar or most recently used.

Certification versus authorization matters here too: some Toolkit resources are available to every Certified Guide, while others are gated behind a specific Specialty Authorization the Guide may not yet hold.
examples: A Guide defaults to a tool they used successfully with a prior Host, without checking whether it actually fits this Host's current stage and need.
lessons.activity: Candidates practice locating three different categories of Toolkit resource and identifying which require a Specialty Authorization they don't yet hold.
lessons.workbook: Describe a tool-selection habit you want to avoid falling into — picking the familiar tool rather than the fitting one.

lessons.title: Preparation
lessons.purpose: Teach appropriate preparation before a Host arrives, while guarding against the Guide pre-deciding what the conversation should cover.
outcomes: Prepare materials and platform readiness appropriately before a session.
Explain the boundary between preparation and pre-deciding the Host's conversation.
teaching: Preparation before a Host arrives includes confirming materials, checking platform readiness, and reviewing whatever context is appropriately available to the Guide.

The critical boundary: preparation must never slide into pre-deciding the Host's conversation. A Guide who arrives with a plan for what the session should cover has already violated Host ownership (Lesson 6.1) before the Host has even spoken.
examples: A Guide reviews available context before a session but consciously avoids forming a plan for 'what we should talk about today' — leaving that entirely to the Host.
lessons.activity: Candidates draft a preparation checklist that includes material and platform readiness but explicitly excludes planning the session's content.
lessons.workbook: Describe the difference between being prepared and having a plan for the Host's conversation.

lessons.title: Opening a New Host Relationship
lessons.purpose: Teach the candidate how a new Host relationship actually begins operationally — orientation, roles, privacy, and consent — before any Journey content starts.
outcomes: Conduct an appropriate orientation for a new Host, covering roles, privacy, and expectations.
Explain what the Host can expect, what the Guide sees, and what remains private, in operational terms.
Establish consent and participation at the relationship's actual start.
teaching: Opening a new Host relationship operationally covers orientation (what AVAIA is and how this will work), roles (Host, Guide, Witness, and how they function), privacy (what the Host can expect regarding what's seen and what stays private), and consent and participation — all before any actual IAP content begins.

This lesson makes concrete what Module 1 and Module 6 taught conceptually: what the Host can expect, what the Guide sees, what remains private, and how the relationship actually begins in real operational terms, on this platform, in this first interaction.

What must happen before IAP begins is the lesson's practical throughline: a Host should never find themselves mid-Awareness-conversation without having first received a clear, honest orientation to what they've entered into.
examples: A new Host logs in for the first time. Before any Journey content begins, the Guide walks through what AVAIA is, what the Host can expect, and confirms consent to proceed.
lessons.activity: Candidates role-play a full new-Host opening sequence, from initial orientation through the first consent check, before any IAP content starts.
lessons.workbook: Draft your own opening orientation script in your own words, covering roles, privacy, and consent.

lessons.title: Journey Operation
lessons.purpose: Teach the operational mechanics of tracking IAP, CAT, and InnerCompass stage status, referrals, and continuity within the platform.
outcomes: Operate platform tools for tracking stage status across IAP, CAT, and InnerCompass.
Execute referrals and continuity handoffs within the platform correctly.
teaching: This lesson makes the conceptual Journey mechanics from Module 2 operational: how stage status is actually tracked and updated on the platform, how referrals between stages are executed, and how continuity is preserved in the platform's own record-keeping, not just in principle.

Candidates practice the actual mechanics here — the conceptual discipline (what carries forward, Room Identity) was already built in Module 2; this lesson is where that discipline becomes a set of concrete platform actions.
examples: A Guide completes an IAP stage and executes the platform referral to CAT, confirming the continuity record accurately reflects what the Host already made visible.
lessons.activity: Candidates practice a full stage-to-stage referral on the platform, verifying continuity information transfers correctly.
lessons.workbook: Describe one way a platform mechanics error (a missed referral, a lost status update) could undermine the continuity principles taught in Module 2.

lessons.title: Privacy in the Actual Interface
lessons.purpose: Make Module 6's privacy architecture concrete within the actual platform interface — what the Host sees, what the Guide sees, and what is intentionally shared.
outcomes: Identify Host-private, Guide-visible, and shared information within the actual platform interface.
Explain what does not automatically carry forward between platform views.
teaching: Module 6, Lesson 6.2 taught privacy architecture conceptually. This lesson locates that same architecture inside the actual interface: which platform views show Host-private information, which show Guide-visible information, and how intentional sharing actually gets executed as a platform action rather than a concept.

What does not automatically carry forward is a key operational point — some information stays siloed between stages or sessions unless deliberately carried forward, and a Guide needs to know the platform's actual default behavior, not assume continuity happens automatically.
language: Privacy architecture, applied to the interface
What does not automatically carry forward
examples: A Guide assumes a note from an earlier session will be visible in the current platform view, but the platform's actual default does not carry it forward automatically — requiring deliberate action.
lessons.activity: Candidates walk through the platform interface identifying which views show which privacy tier of information.
lessons.workbook: Write down one assumption you might make about what 'automatically' carries forward on the platform, and verify it against what actually happens.

lessons.title: Workbook & Continuity
lessons.purpose: Teach the operational mechanics of the Host's Workbook and its role in continuity across stages and sessions.
outcomes: Navigate the Workbook's role in platform continuity.
Explain the Workbook's privacy status relative to other platform information.
teaching: The Workbook is the Host's own space, distinct from Guide-visible session content, and plays a specific role in continuity — what the Host has written there may or may not carry forward into later stages depending on platform mechanics and the Host's own choices about sharing it.
This lesson operationalizes the privacy-tier distinction from Lesson 6.2: the Workbook is explicitly Host-private material unless and until the Host chooses otherwise.
examples: A Host has written extensively in their Workbook. A Guide does not treat that content as available for discussion unless the Host brings it forward.
lessons.activity: Candidates trace how Workbook content does and does not surface across different platform views.
lessons.workbook: Reflect on how you'll explain the Workbook's privacy status to a new Host in plain language.

lessons.title: Library
lessons.purpose: Orient the candidate to the Library as a resource location distinct from the Toolkit, and teach appropriate navigation.
outcomes: Navigate the Library to locate appropriate participant and Guide materials.
Distinguish Library resources from Toolkit resources (Lesson 7.2).
teaching: The Library holds reference and supporting materials distinct from the Toolkit's conversation and process tools — candidates need basic fluency locating what's there and understanding how it differs functionally from the Toolkit.
examples: A Guide looking for background reference material for a Host checks the Library, while a Guide looking for a conversation-structuring tool checks the Toolkit.
lessons.activity: Candidates practice locating three different Library resources and identifying how each differs functionally from a Toolkit resource.
lessons.workbook: Describe, in your own words, the functional difference between the Library and the Toolkit.

lessons.title: Materials
lessons.purpose: Teach the candidate to locate, prepare, and appropriately use participant and Guide materials for a session.
outcomes: Locate and prepare appropriate materials for a given session.
Distinguish participant materials from Guide-only materials.
teaching: Beyond the Toolkit and Library as resource locations, this lesson covers the practical task of locating, preparing, and printing or otherwise readying materials for actual use in a session — separating what's meant for the participant (Host) from what's meant for the Guide alone.
examples: A Guide preparing for a session correctly identifies which materials are meant to be shared directly with the Host and which are Guide-only reference.
lessons.activity: Candidates prepare a sample materials set for a hypothetical session, correctly separating participant materials from Guide-only materials.
lessons.workbook: List the materials you expect to need most often as a new Guide, and note which are participant-facing.

lessons.title: Programs, Experiences & Authorization
lessons.purpose: Teach the candidate to distinguish core certification from program-level authorization, so they understand what they are and are not yet qualified to facilitate.
outcomes: Distinguish certification from program or experience-specific authorization.
Identify which programs or experiences require authorization beyond core certification.
teaching: Core certification qualifies a Guide to steward the AVAIA Journey as taught in this curriculum. Certain programs and experiences — Specialty Authorizations like Defying Grief, Unsung Heroes, View From Above, Shared Room, and Youth — require authorization beyond core certification, earned separately afterward.
A Certified Guide needs to recognize which programs fall inside their current authorization and which don't, so they never inadvertently facilitate something they're not yet qualified for.
examples: A newly certified Guide is asked to facilitate a Shared Room experience. They correctly recognize this requires a Specialty Authorization they don't yet hold.
lessons.activity: Candidates review a list of programs and experiences and sort them into 'core certification covers this' and 'requires additional authorization.'
lessons.workbook: List which Specialty Authorizations, if any, you're interested in pursuing after core certification, and why.

lessons.title: Operational & Technology Failure
lessons.purpose: Teach the candidate to handle platform and technology failures without compromising privacy, ownership, or AVAIA's architecture through improvised workarounds.
outcomes: Respond appropriately to platform failure, microphone failure, transcription errors, connection loss, incorrect status, and inability to locate something.
Apply the governing rule: technology problems do not authorize workarounds around privacy, ownership, or AVAIA architecture.
Preserve the human conversation through a technical failure.
teaching: Technology will sometimes fail: platform outages, microphone issues, transcription errors, connection loss, an incorrect status display, or simply being unable to locate something needed in the moment. These are operational problems, not justification for bypassing AVAIA's structure.

The governing rule is absolute: technology problems do not authorize workarounds around privacy, ownership, or AVAIA architecture. A Guide facing a platform failure does not, for instance, resort to an unapproved outside tool or channel to keep the conversation going, however well-intentioned.

Preserving the human conversation through a technical failure means staying present with the Host, acknowledging the disruption honestly, and following approved recovery steps — rather than letting a technical problem become a Host-facing crisis of its own.
language: “Technology problems do not authorize workarounds around privacy, ownership, or AVAIA architecture”
Preserving the human conversation through failure
examples: A platform outage interrupts a session. Rather than moving the conversation to an unapproved personal messaging app to 'keep going,' the Guide pauses, communicates honestly with the Host, and follows the approved recovery path.
lessons.activity: Candidates work through three scripted technology-failure scenarios, practicing a recovery response that never bypasses privacy or architecture.
lessons.workbook: Write your own plain-language explanation you could give a Host if a technical failure interrupted your session together.

lessons.title: Journey Completion in the Platform
lessons.purpose: Teach the operational mechanics of marking a Journey's completion status in the platform, and connect it back to the conceptual completion material from Module 2.
outcomes: Execute operational completion status changes in the platform correctly.
Ensure Host continuity remains intact through a platform completion action.
Connect platform-level completion to the conceptual completion taught in Lesson 2.7.
teaching: Marking operational completion, status, and follow-forward behavior in the platform is the mechanical counterpart to Lesson 2.7's conceptual treatment of what completion does and does not mean. This lesson teaches the actual platform actions: how completion status gets recorded, and what follow-forward behavior actually exists afterward.

Ensuring Host continuity remains intact through this action matters because a careless platform completion action could sever continuity the Host would want preserved — this lesson teaches the Guide to execute completion correctly, not just conceptually understand it.

The relationship to conceptual completion from Module 2 should stay explicit throughout: this lesson does not introduce a new idea of what completion means, only the mechanics of recording it accurately.
examples: A Guide marks a Journey complete in the platform, confirming the continuity and follow-forward settings accurately reflect what should remain available if the Host returns later.
lessons.activity: Candidates practice executing a platform-level Journey completion for a sample case, verifying continuity settings remain correct afterward.
lessons.workbook: Describe how you'll make sure a platform completion action doesn't accidentally undercut what Lesson 2.7 taught about completion not meaning 'finished.'

lessons.title: Guide Transition & Host Continuity: Operational Mechanics

practiceLabs.title: IAP: You Get to Say It
practiceLabs.competency: Remain in Awareness while allowing the Host's experience to emerge associatively.

host.text: You recently left a job you had held for 11 years.
You initially tell the Guide:
“I thought leaving would feel better than this.”
You are not sure what bothers you most.
During the conversation, naturally mention:

items: wondering whether leaving was a mistake

host.text: Do not present these neatly. Move between them as you naturally might while trying to make sense of something.
